headline: Consumers Refuse to Let AI Book Their Rides; AI Now Just Sits There, Quietly Calculating
subheadline: Despite billions invested in 'agentic commerce', AI shopping agents account for a rounding error of transactions, as humans stubbornly continue ordering their own burritos like cavemen.
author: Dexter Appiah-Clarke, Markets & Meaning Desk
seoTitle: Consumers Reject AI Shopping Agents En Masse | The Daily Absurd
seoDescription: Satire: billions were invested in AI agents that shop and book for you. Consumers have responded by simply continuing to do it themselves.
sourceEvent: Despite heavy investment in agentic commerce, third-party AI shopping agents reportedly account for only a tiny share of Uber and DoorDash transactions, and travel platforms report similarly limited adoption.

social.x: Tech spent billions building AI agents to order your burritos. Consumers looked at this offer and ordered their own burritos. Investors are calling it 'a failure to understand the market', the market is calling it 'lunch'.
social.facebook: AI agents were supposed to book our rides and buy our stuff. Turns out we'd rather tap the burrito button ourselves. An industry reckons with rejection.
social.instagram: The AI agent era: machines fully ready to spend your money, humans fully unwilling to let them. #satire #ai
altHeadlines: AI Agents Offer to Do Your Shopping; Humanity Politely Declines Forever
Agentic Commerce Reports 0.03% Adoption, 100% Investor Confidence Anyway

body:
Silicon Valley was in mourning this week after reports confirmed that AI shopping agents — the crown jewel of the 'agentic commerce' revolution — account for only a tiny share of transactions on platforms like Uber and DoorDash, as consumers overwhelmingly prefer the medieval ritual of pressing the burrito button themselves.

The technology, developed at a cost roughly equivalent to the GDP of a mid-sized European nation, was designed to autonomously order food, book rides and schedule travel. It has instead been adopted primarily by investors' presentations.

"We built an agent that can negotiate with an airline, optimise your route and expense the receipt," said one disappointed product lead. "Users' response has been to open the app and click 'same as last time' in about four seconds. We cannot compete with 'same as last time'. It is the perfect interface. It has no onboarding."

Analysts note the rejection may reflect a deep consumer insight the industry overlooked: people do not want an AI to spend their money. They want to spend it themselves, badly, on things they do not need, the way nature intended.

"I tried letting the agent handle dinner," said one early adopter in Melbourne. "It ordered a 'nutritionally optimal' meal for the family. The kids unionised. Never again."

Undeterred, the industry has announced it will pivot to the next frontier: AI agents that convince consumers they wanted AI agents. Preliminary testing suggests the agents are already highly effective, having convinced investors to spend billions on AI agents.

At press time, your correspondent's delivery app suggested ordering 'the usual'. It was, as always, correct — the only intelligence anyone actually needed.
